# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by the extracellular deposition of misfolded amyloid protein fibrils within the myocardium [1]. Once considered rare and untreatable, CA is now recognized as an increasingly diagnosed and treatable cause of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) [2]. The two predominant forms affecting the heart are light-chain (AL) amyloidosis, arising from a clonal plasma cell dyscrasia, and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, which may be hereditary (ATTRv) or wild-type (ATTRwt) [3]. Increased awareness and advances in noninvasive imaging have transformed the diagnostic landscape over the past decade [4].

## Epidemiology and Pathophysiology

ATTRwt amyloidosis predominantly affects older men and is increasingly identified among patients hospitalized for HFpEF, aortic stenosis, and unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy [5]. Autopsy studies suggest that ATTRwt deposition may be present in up to 25% of individuals over the age of 80 [6]. AL amyloidosis, by contrast, is less common but more aggressive, with rapid clinical deterioration if untreated [7]. The hereditary ATTRv form is associated with specific TTR gene variants, including the V122I (p.V142I) mutation prevalent among individuals of West African ancestry [8].

The pathophysiology involves amyloid fibril infiltration causing progressive ventricular wall thickening, diastolic dysfunction, and ultimately restrictive cardiomyopathy [9]. In AL amyloidosis, circulating light chains exert direct cardiotoxic effects independent of fibril deposition, contributing to the disproportionate clinical severity [10].

## Clinical Presentation

CA commonly presents with progressive heart failure, fatigue, and reduced exercise tolerance [11]. Several "red flags" should raise suspicion, including bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, and discordance between low-voltage electrocardiograms and increased wall thickness on echocardiography [12]. Autonomic and peripheral neuropathy frequently accompany ATTRv disease [13]. Conduction system disease and atrial arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation, are common [14].

## Diagnosis

Echocardiography typically reveals increased biventricular wall thickness, granular myocardial texture, biatrial enlargement, and a characteristic apical-sparing pattern of longitudinal strain ("cherry-on-top") [15]. Cardiac magnetic resonance demonstrates diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement and elevated native T1 and extracellular volume [16].

A major advance has been the use of bone-avid radiotracer scintigraphy (technetium-labeled pyrophosphate or DPD) to diagnose ATTR-CA noninvasively [17]. Grade 2–3 myocardial uptake in the absence of a monoclonal protein has high specificity for ATTR-CA, often obviating the need for endomyocardial biopsy [18]. Critically, monoclonal protein screening with serum and urine immunofixation and serum free light chain assays is mandatory to exclude AL amyloidosis before attributing positive scintigraphy to ATTR [19]. Genetic testing distinguishes ATTRv from ATTRwt and informs family screening [20]. Endomyocardial biopsy with Congo red staining and amyloid typing by mass spectrometry remains the gold standard when noninvasive criteria are not met [21].

## Treatment

Management of AL-CA centers on rapid suppression of the underlying plasma cell clone. Regimens incorporating bortezomib and, more recently, the anti-CD38 antibody daratumumab have improved hematologic and organ responses [22]. The ANDROMEDA trial established daratumumab-based therapy as a standard of care in newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis [23].

For ATTR-CA, the transthyretin stabilizer tafamidis was shown in the ATTR-ACT trial to reduce all-cause mortality and cardiovascular hospitalizations [24]. Subsequently, gene-silencing therapies targeting hepatic TTR production have emerged: patisiran and inotersen demonstrated efficacy in ATTRv polyneuropathy [25,26]. More recently, the HELIOS-B trial showed that vutrisiran, a subcutaneous small interfering RNA agent, reduced death and cardiovascular events in ATTR-CA [27]. Acoramidis, a next-generation stabilizer, demonstrated clinical benefit in the ATTRibute-CM trial [28]. Investigational CRISPR-based in vivo gene editing has shown durable reductions in serum TTR, representing a potentially transformative approach [29].

Supportive heart failure management relies on cautious diuresis; conventional agents such as beta-blockers and renin-angiotensin inhibitors are often poorly tolerated. Anticoagulation is generally recommended for atrial fibrillation given elevated thromboembolic risk [30].

## Conclusion

Cardiac amyloidosis has evolved from an underrecognized and uniformly fatal disorder into a diagnosable and increasingly treatable condition. The integration of red-flag recognition, multimodality imaging, and noninvasive scintigraphic diagnosis, combined with the advent of disease-modifying therapies, has dramatically improved outcomes. Early diagnosis remains paramount, as therapeutic benefit is greatest before irreversible cardiac damage occurs. Continued advances in gene silencing and editing promise further progress in the years ahead.
